source.title: A modular semantic-structural pipeline for visual decoding from primate spiking data via selective temporal integration
source.authors: Matteo Ciferri; M. Ferrante; N. Toschi

record.file_problem: The supplied title differs from the title printed in the paper. The text itself is a complete paper with appendix and is not garbled or cut off.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports scaling of primate neural-decoding retrieval accuracy, not language-model held-out loss, parameter/token/compute scaling, or compute-optimal allocation. Its results do not test the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper's scaling experiments vary PCA input dimensionality and training-set size and measure image-retrieval accuracy. They do not measure language-model cross-entropy loss or test model-size, token, compute, or compute-optimal allocation laws. The scaling results are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study decodes images from macaque intracortical recordings and charts Top-1/Top-5 retrieval accuracy against PCA input dimensionality and training-set size, with log-fit curves. It does not measure model loss against parameters, tokens or compute. It does not fit compute-optimal allocation, vary architecture shape at fixed size, or test language-model downstream tasks. Its 'scaling law' label refers to diminishing-returns accuracy trends in a small neural decoder, which is a related but different construct from any version. V5 requires the power-law loss form in another modality or regime with model/data scale. Here the measure is retrieval accuracy, and one axis is input dimensionality, so it does not bear on V5 either.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors say retrieval accuracy improves predictably with more PCA input dimensions and more training trials, with diminishing returns. They draw design guidance from this: more diverse trials help most, and higher channel count helps too. Their main conclusion is that temporal modelling, not architectural complexity, drives decoding accuracy.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies neural input dimensionality and training-set size and measures image-retrieval accuracy; it does not use language-model loss scaling fits or compute-optimal allocation methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports diminishing returns beyond 256 PCA dimensions and beyond 10,000 training samples; it does not report sensitivity of language-model scaling fits to setup or fitting choices.

fits_no_version.finding: In macaque MUA-to-CLIP decoding, Top-1 and Top-5 retrieval accuracy rise roughly logarithmically with PCA input dimensionality, with diminishing returns beyond ~256 components (figure only).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neural-decoding retrieval accuracy grows roughly logarithmically with input dimensionality, with diminishing returns.

fits_no_version.finding: Retrieval accuracy rises log-linearly with training-set size, steeply between 100 and 5000 samples, tapering beyond 10,000. Top-5 reaches ~90% near 15,000 samples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neural-decoding retrieval accuracy grows log-linearly with number of training trials, with diminishing returns.

record.problems: The scaling plots are not accompanied by numerical points, fitted coefficients, or reported uncertainty. The paper also notes that the data are limited to a few subjects and a single modality.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation of fits from small to much larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameters and data.
No depth/width comparison at fixed parameter count.

Neural-decoding setting, but measures retrieval accuracy versus PCA dimensions and trial count, not loss scaling with model or data scale. Fit form is logarithmic, not power-law, and no coefficients are given.
No language-model downstream performance versus scale or pretraining loss.
No comparison of exponents or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: Rows R1–R4 correctly have versions ['none']. Their 'observed' state refers to the study's own trend, not any claim version. No numerical fit values or R2 are reported, so the scaling plots cannot be compared quantitatively. The paper cites Kaplan et al. only as an analogy. The title mismatch noted by the reader is a metadata issue.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not measure held-out language-model pretraining loss against parameter count, tokens, or compute.
The paper does not fit language-model loss curves on smaller runs or test predictions on larger runs.
The paper does not vary model parameters and training tokens under fixed compute or estimate a compute-optimal split.
The paper does not test architecture effects on language-model loss at fixed parameter count.

The paper studies visual decoding from neural recordings, but measures retrieval accuracy rather than the claimed power-law loss form; it does not test the same loss scaling in another modality or training regime.
The paper does not test language-model downstream-task performance against scale or pretraining loss.
The paper does not assess language-model scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits across fitting choices.

tranche.reason: The experiments measure logarithmic retrieval-accuracy trends against neural input dimensionality and decoder training-set size. They neither test the specified power-law claims nor use those laws as a tool.
